summary: Covers emergency calls where only application data must be sent and no interactive media channel is set up, such as an automatic crash notification. It builds on the framework for emergency calling in RFC 6443 and is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a call for help needs only a short message with details, not a conversation. This document explains how a device can send that automatically to emergency services.

questions: how do devices send automatic emergency messages
what is a non-interactive emergency call
how does cap work with sip message
subtitle: How a sensor or other device can send an emergency alert, with data only and no voice or video session.

tldr.problem: Some emergency calls carry only application data, such as a sensor alert, and have no interactive voice, video or text, so setting up a full SIP INVITE session is unnecessary.
tldr.mechanism: The device sends a SIP MESSAGE transaction that carries a Common Alerting Protocol (CAP) alert, either in the body or by reference in a Call-Info header field. The RFC also adds a 425 response and an AlertMsg-Error header field for bad alerts.
tldr.outcome: Routing and processing follow ordinary emergency calls, but no session is created. The RFC defines no callback method and no rate limiting.

today: RFC 8876 is a Proposed Standard, published in September 2020, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the emergency calling framework in RFC 6443.

sections.title: Emergency Calls Without Media
sections.content:
RFC 6443 describes how devices place emergency calls over the Internet and how Public Safety Answering Points (PSAPs) handle them. Those calls normally start with a SIP INVITE that sets up a session. But sometimes only application data needs to reach a PSAP or an intermediary, as with sensors issuing alerts and certain medical monitors.

The RFC calls these non-interactive emergency calls: emergency calls with no two-way interactive media such as voice, video or real-time text. They still need emergency indications, emergency call routing and location. The data format is the Common Alerting Protocol (CAP), which is normally used between authorities and to the public. This document uses it to carry alerts from private devices to emergency service authorities.
sections.plainLanguage: A smoke alarm does not need to talk. It only needs to send a short message with the details, so this document shows how.

sections.title: Two Routing Modes
sections.content:
The RFC describes targeted and location-based routing. In targeted routing, a pre-configured sensor sends the alert to an aggregator, which decides what to do next. It might send a data-only call toward a PSAP or start a third-party-initiated emergency call with audio, video and data. A security firm is the RFC's example.

In location-based routing, the alert is addressed to a service URN (the example uses urn:service:sos) because the sender does not know the recipient. An Emergency Services Routing Proxy (ESRP) may use LoST to find the next hop toward a PSAP. The only difference from a classic voice emergency call is that this one uses MESSAGE instead of INVITE, creates no session and has no interactive media.
sections.plainLanguage: The alarm can send its note to a company that decides what to do, or to a general emergency address that gets it to the right local office.

sections.title: Carrying a CAP Alert in SIP MESSAGE
sections.content:
Only the SIP MESSAGE transaction is defined for this purpose. Behavior with other transactions is not defined. The CAP alert travels as an additional data block (RFC 7852) announced in a Call-Info header field with the purpose EmergencyCallData.cap. The header can hold a URI for fetching the alert, or a Content-ID URL with the alert in a MIME body part of type application/emergencyCallData.cap+xml.

If the server cannot support the request it returns 501 Not Implemented. If it cannot handle the body format it returns 415 Unsupported Media Type and MUST list acceptable formats. Apart from not creating a session or interactive media, the headers, routing and processing match other emergency calls, as in RFC 6881.
sections.plainLanguage: The alert is attached to the message like a note in an envelope, or the message just says where to go to read it.

sections.title: Rules for the CAP Content
sections.content:
CAP use MUST conform to the CAP specification, with extra rules for SIP.

  • sender: set to the SIP URI of the user agent when a SIP entity created the alert; keep the original identity for a non-SIP originator; and do not use the user agent's SIP URI when the distinct author matters.
  • incidents: MUST be present and unique for a given sender, expires, incidents combination.
  • scope: MAY be "Private". The addresses element is not used, because SIP already carries addressing.
  • parameter: MAY hold sender-specific extra information.
  • area: RECOMMENDED to omit. If present, the location SHOULD be copied into a PIDF-LO referenced by the Geolocation header field.

When building area from a PIDF-LO, points SHOULD become circles with a radius equal to the uncertainty, arc-bands and ellipses SHOULD become polygons, and 3D locations SHOULD be flattened to 2D.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a checklist for filling in the alert form so everyone reads it the same way, such as who sent it and a unique number for the incident.

sections.title: The 425 Response and AlertMsg-Error
sections.content:
The RFC adds the 425 (Bad Alert Message) response, meaning the request was so malformed that no reasonable emergency response can be determined. A 425 MUST include an AlertMsg-Error header field. It should be used only when the responder has no other usable information, MUST NOT be sent for a request that lacks an alert at all, and is a final response that MUST NOT end an existing dialog.

AlertMsg-Error holds exactly one 3-digit error code with an optional, recommended message text. The code space is separate from SIP status codes. It may appear in any response, so a PSAP can accept a MESSAGE with 200 OK and still report that the alert was bad. In provisional responses it MUST use the mechanism of RFC 3262 or be repeated in the final response. If an entity cannot or will not process the alert, a 500 SHOULD be used, with or without a Retry-After header field.
sections.plainLanguage: If the alert is so garbled that nobody can tell what happened, the receiver sends back a special "bad alert" reply with a number that says what was wrong.

sections.title: Callbacks and Large Data
sections.content:
No method is described for calling back the sender. Such alerts are usually sent by automata that cannot receive calls. The From identifier may help find more information, and the CAP alert may contain contact details.

Sending tens of kilobytes in a MESSAGE is not advisable, because SIP entities are usually not equipped for very large messages. The sender SHOULD instead use the by-reference mechanisms of RFC 7852: publish the data over HTTPS and put its URI in Call-Info. The CAP alert and any sensor-specific data blocks can be sent this way. No SIP rate-limiting mechanism is standardized, and because a human call-taker is typically involved, implementers should take note, especially for automatic calls.
sections.plainLanguage: Big files are not stuffed into the message. The message just points to where they can be picked up.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives two messages. In the first, a sensor named sensor1@example.com sends a SIP MESSAGE to an aggregator with a CAP document reporting a BURGLARY event. Its location comes from the Geolocation header field and a PIDF-LO body part, and it also carries proprietary sensor data in CAP parameter elements.

In the second, the aggregator sends the same CAP document as a MESSAGE to urn:service:sos with a Route header field toward a PSAP.
sections.plainLanguage: A burglar alarm sends its note to a monitoring company, which then forwards the same note to the emergency office.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Alerts from sensors may be false, for example when a sensor malfunctions, so they are not always sent straight to a PSAP and may be filtered or correlated by a separate entity. Identity can matter in deciding whether to accept an alert. SIP offers P-Asserted-Identity and SIP Identity, and CAP has its own signing mechanisms. The specific policy is out of scope.

SIP has no rate limiting, so these calls could be abused for denial of service against emergency services. Automated emergency calls may be regulated, with penalties for false positives, in some jurisdictions. Recipients MUST take precautions when fetching by-reference data, because the URI may point to a malicious party. Replay can be detected through the CAP identifier, sender, sent and optional expire elements. Using SIP Identity PASSporT and TLS is RECOMMENDED. None of this protects against a compromised sensor sending crafted alerts.
sections.plainLanguage: A broken or sneaky alarm could send fake alerts, so receivers need ways to check who sent a message and to avoid being flooded.
